newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian probe urges new local call limits.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian probe urges new local call limits.

text.p: An Australian Senate committee investigating the government's new system of telecommunications regulation recommended on Wednesday that Telstra Corp be required to share the benefits of local-call competition among all customers.

The committee's majority report, written by three government senators including the committee chair, urged that the nationwide ceiling on Telstra's local-call charges be reduced if necessary to reflect discounting in areas with competition in the local-call market.
Because competition in the local-call market requires duplicate cabling and switching it is not expected to spread to all of Australia, raising the possibility of prices falling in only some places.
The duplication that is expected will rely on pay television services distributed by an affiliate of Optus Communications Pty Ltd, Telstra's chief competitor.
The Senate last year asked the committee to examine the package of bills that would create the new system of largely open-market telecommuncations competition after July 1.
The committee also had two senators from the opposition Labor Party and one from the Australian Democrats, which usually join Labor in opposing government legislation.

The minority report of those three senators was not immediately available but would normally reflect the demands of those parties when the new bills come up for amendment in the Seante, which the Liberal-National government does not control.
The majority senators also recommended that:
-- Communications Minister Richard Alston review allegations of exploitation of untimed local calls, for example, when people use them to connect data services for long periods.
-- The bill be amended to prevent such exploitation and the resulting cross-subsidisation between customers.
-- A rise in telecoms carriers' liability for falling short of performance standards to A$25,000 from A$3,000.
-- Internet providers be subject to the industry ombudsman.
-- Carriers be required to restore sites they disturb when installing facilities.
-- Telstra be required to fulfill its promise to provide 93.4 percent of its customers with digital data capability by 2000.
-- The minister examine the merits of all Australians gaining digital data access by 2000.
The government plans to sell a third of Telstra in the fiscal year to June 1998.
Optus Communications' equity is held by Mayne Nickless Ltd with 25 percent, Cable and Wireless Plc (24.5 percent), BellSouth Corp (24.5 percent) and several Australian institutional investors.
